en: *Daśabhāṇavāra-karmavācanā: Essentials for Bhikṣus*, one fascicle;
compiled by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Śīla Saṃghapuṣpa at Zhongxing Monastery in Yangdu, based on the Vinaya.

Karmavācanās are numerous according to their specific matters; for now, I shall briefly set forth the essential ones based on established texts, while those not fully covered here remain in the original compendium.
Whenever one intends to perform a karmavācanā within the great assembly, the presiding officer shall call for the gathering:
"The Saṃgha is now assembled in harmony; what matter do you wish to perform?"
One person among the Sangha should respond accordingly by performing the specific *karmavācanā*, and then announce:

"The monks who have not arrived have declared their consent (*chanda*); having finished declaring it, I shall now perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*). If this is taking place within the boundary of the *sīmā*, one simply makes the announcement.
“Monks, you are now gathered in harmony; what matter do you wish to perform?

**Text for Receiving the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, Part One: The Method for Receiving the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts** When a layperson first comes wishing to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, they are instructed to pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. They then kneel with their right knee on the ground (hukuei), join their palms, and repent for the three types of karma. Only after this should they receive the precepts.

The Preceptor should instruct them, saying: "I, [Name], from this time forth for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among the two-legged; I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Honored One among the assemblies."
Thus it is said three times: "I, [name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, have completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
Within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, I joyfully accept the five precepts and become an upāsaka."
"You should understand this.
Thus it is said three times: "Listen, [Name]!
This Buddha, the Bhagavān, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the five precepts for the upāsaka."
All upāsakas should protect and uphold [these precepts] for as long as they live.
What are the five? To abstain from taking life for as long as one lives is the upāsaka precept.
"Regarding this, can you maintain the precept of abstaining from taking life for as long as you live?
He replied, "I can. "Abstaining from taking what is not given for as long as you live is a lay follower's (upāsaka) precept."
"Among these, can you maintain the precept of abstaining from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts?
"I can. "Abstaining from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts is a lay follower's (upāsaka) precept.
Among these, can you maintain the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts?"
He replied, “I am able. “To abstain from false speech for as long as life lasts is a lay follower’s precept (*upāsaka-śīla*).
Regarding this matter of abstaining from false speech for as long as life lasts, are you able to maintain it?
He replied, “I am able. “To abstain from drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts is a lay follower’s precept.”

Among these, for as long as life lasts, you must abstain from drinking intoxicants—whether liquor made from grain, liquor made from sugarcane, liquor made from grapes, or any other substance capable of causing heedlessness. Can you maintain this?

**The Text for Receiving the Eight Precepts, Part Two.** When someone comes wishing to receive the eight precepts, first instruct them to pay homage to the Triple Gem; thereafter, instruct them to kneel with their right knee on the ground and join their palms.

The preceptor should instruct [the candidate] to speak as follows: "I, [name], from now until tomorrow morning, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among assemblies."

Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], from now until tomorrow morning, have completed my taking refuge in the Buddha, have completed my taking refuge in the Dharma, and have completed my taking refuge in the Saṃgha."
Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], have completed receiving the Three Refuges.
From beginningless saṃsāra until this day, my unwholesome bodily karma—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and my unwholesome vocal karma—"
False speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued speech; unwholesome mental karma:

covetousness, malice and anger, and deluded false views—toward all these various transgressions, I now seek compassionate repentance before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the venerable Bodhisattvas, the worthy sages who have attained the Way, and the present teachers and monks.
I, [Name], have finished my confession; my physical actions are pure, my verbal actions are pure, and my mental actions are pure—this is called dwelling in purity.

From now until tomorrow morning, I shall train in the ways of all Buddhas: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, not drinking intoxicants, not sitting or lying on high, wide, or large beds, not wearing perfumes, flowers, necklaces, or anointing the body with fragrant oils, not going to see or listen to singing, music, or performances, and not eating after midday.
Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], have now completed receiving the eight precepts.

By this merit, I do not seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor the kings of Śakra, Brahmā, or other human and celestial realms; rather, I vow to exhaust all afflictions, clearly understand all dharmas, and ultimately attain the Buddha-way."

The *upāsikā*’s acceptance of the text is also like this. The Text for Requesting the Ritual for Keeping Disciples (The Third Text for Requesting the Ritual for Keeping Disciples): When a *bhikṣuṇī* who has completed twelve years since her full ordination wishes to keep disciples, she should assemble the Saṃgha, kneel with palms joined, and request as follows: “May the venerable *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha listen! [...]”
I, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], having received the full ordination for twelve years, wish to take on disciples.
I, [Name], have already requested the *karmavācanā* for taking on disciples from the Saṃgha; may the Saṃgha grant me, [Name], the *karmavācanā* for taking on disciples.

“Out of compassion. Thus it is said three times. The *karmavācanā* for granting permission to maintain a following: “Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen! [... The *karmavācanā* for granting permission to maintain a following: “Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!”
The bhikṣuṇī [Name], having received full ordination for twelve years, wishes to maintain a group of disciples.
[Name] has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for maintaining a group of disciples.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, the Saṃgha shall grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for [Name] to keep disciples.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Nuns of the Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣuṇī [Name], having received the full ordination for twelve years, wishes to maintain a group of disciples.
[Name] has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for maintaining a group of disciples; the Saṃgha now grants [Name] the formal act for maintaining a group of disciples.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for such-and-such a person to maintain a retinue should remain silent;
those who do not consent should speak.
Is this first formal act accomplished?"
Thus it was said three times: "The Sangha has already granted the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for [the name] to keep a retinue.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
4. The Text for Receiving the Ten Śrāmaṇera Precepts. The Fourth Text for Receiving the Ten Śrāmaṇera Precepts.
The Buddha said: “O Bhikṣus!
From this day forward, those who wish to seek the life of one who has gone forth must report two matters to the Saṃgha.”
Once one has gone forth and shaved the head, if the hair has already been shorn, one thing must be reported to the Saṃgha.
When the Saṃgha is assembled, one should say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"Such-and-such a person seeks to go forth and have their hair shaved.
May the Sangha bear this in mind!
If the Sangha is not assembled, one should inform them in a separate room, saying: "Venerable elders!..."
"Such-and-such a person seeks to go forth;
please remember this!
If there is a *kāṣāya*, it should be put on.
If there is no [other candidate], the preceptor should provide one himself; he should instruct [the candidate] to kneel with palms joined and first teach him how to request the preceptor, saying:
"Venerable Sir, please take heed! I, so-and-so, request the Venerable Sir to be my preceptor for the śrāmaṇera ordination; may the Venerable Sir act as my preceptor for the ten precepts."
"I, [Name], relying upon the Venerable Preceptor, go forth from the household life and receive the ten precepts.
Thus it is said three times.
The Preceptor should instruct: "I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha; I go forth."
When this Buddha Bhagavān Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, went forth from home, I also followed the Buddha to go forth, with [Name] as my preceptor.
Thus it is said three times: "I, [Name], having taken refuge in the Buddha, having taken refuge in the Dharma, and having taken refuge in the Saṃgha, go forth.
I go forth as a renunciant under the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I too have completed going forth following the Buddha, with [Name] as my preceptor."
The Preceptor should say: "Listen, [Name]!
This Buddha, the Bhagavān Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras."
What are the ten? "To abstain from taking life for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this abstention from taking life for as long as one lives, are you able to uphold it?"
[The preceptor] replies: "To abstain from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this abstention from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts, are you able to maintain it?
[The candidate] replies: "I am able. "To abstain from unchaste conduct for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept."
"Within this, you must abstain from unchaste conduct for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replies, "I can. "To abstain from false speech for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, you must abstain from false speech for as long as you live; can you maintain this?"
He replied, "To abstain from drinking intoxicants for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, to abstain from drinking intoxicants for as long as one lives—including rice wine, sugarcane wine, grape wine, and all other intoxicants that lead to heedlessness—can you maintain this?"
He replied, "I can. [The preceptor said: "To abstain from sitting or lying on high, wide, and large beds for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this abstention from sitting or lying on high, wide, and large beds for as long as life lasts, are you able to maintain it?"
He replied, "I can. [The preceptor said: "To abstain from wearing flowers, incense, garlands, and from anointing the body with fragrant oils for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, you must abstain from wearing flowers, incense, garlands, and from anointing the body with fragrant oils for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold this?"

He replied, "I can. [The preceptor said: "To abstain for as long as life lasts from going to see or listen to performances involving singing, chanting, or instrumental music—this is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this abstention for as long as life lasts from going to see or listen to performances involving singing, chanting, or instrumental music, are you able to maintain it?"
He replied, "I can. [The preceptor said: "To abstain from receiving, accepting, or storing gold, silver, money, or treasures for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, you must abstain from receiving, accepting, or storing gold, silver, money, or treasures for as long as you live; are you able to uphold this?"
He replied, "I am able. [The teacher said: "Abstaining from eating at improper times for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, are you able to maintain abstention from eating at improper times for as long as life lasts?
He replied, "I am able. "In this way, these ten śrāmaṇera precepts must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts."

You should diligently make offerings to the Three Jewels—the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Bhikṣu Saṃgha Jewel; you should make offerings to your preceptors and ācāryas. You must not disobey any instruction that accords with the Dharma, but should diligently seek out skillful means through study, seated meditation, and recitation of the sūtras. Within the Buddha-Dharma, you shall attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, and even attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus, let your renunciation not be in vain, and let the fruition of its rewards never cease.
That which you do not understand, your Upādhyāyī and Ācāryā shall explain to you in detail.

The ritual texts for the Upāsikā’s triple refuge and five precepts, as well as the eight precepts, and the Śrāmaṇerikā’s triple refuge and ten precepts, are entirely identical to the aforementioned ritual text for the ordination of the Śrāmaṇera’s ten precepts; the only difference here is that one refers to her as a “Śrāmaṇerikā. 5. The Ritual Text for Receiving the Six Dharmas at the Altar (Fifth). If a Śrāmaṇerikā first arrives, she should be instructed to perform prostrations with her head to the feet of the Saṃgha in due order, after which she should successively request an Upādhyāyinī.
The Preceptor instructs, saying: "Venerable One, please take heed!
I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], request you, Venerable One, to be my upādhyāyī; may you, Venerable One, act as my upādhyāyī."
"I, [Name], because of my preceptor nun, have been granted two years of training by the Saṃgha.
Thus she should say three times. A bhikṣuṇī should then ask the preceptor nun:
"Are you able to act as the preceptor for [Name]?"
He replies, “I can.
One should then lead him to the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā*), placing him where he is within sight but beyond hearing.
At that time, one should ask: “Is the Saṃgha in harmony?”
The Saṃgha, being of one mind and in harmony, shall perform the business of the Saṃgha.
The preceptor-ni [Name], for the śrāmaṇerī [Name], the Saṃgha shall grant her two years of training in the precepts.
Thus it is said three times.

If the Saṃgha is united in one mind, they should summon the śrāmaṇerikā and instruct her to prostrate herself, bowing her head at each of the feet of the Saṃgha. Next, she should be instructed to request the two-year training in the precepts from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows: "Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!"
I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with [Name] as my preceptress (upādhyāyinī), request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as my preceptress.
May the Saṃgha grant me, [Name], the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as my preceptress.
"Out of compassion.
Thus he requests three times.
Thereupon, the Preceptor of the Precepts should announce within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Bhikṣuṇīs of the Saṃgha, listen!"
The śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name], requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] as her preceptor.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission; the Saṃgha shall grant [Name] the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] as her preceptor.
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
The śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name], requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] as her preceptor."
The Saṃgha now grants [the name] So-and-so two years of training in the precepts, with the Bhikṣuṇī So-and-so as Preceptor.
Which Elders consent to granting So-and-so two years of training in the precepts, with the Bhikṣuṇī So-and-so as Preceptor? Those who consent, let them remain silent;
those who do not consent, let them speak.
"Has this first *karmavācanā* been accomplished?
Thus it is said three times: "The Saṃgha has already granted the two-year training in the precepts to [Name], with [Name] as her preceptor-nun."
"Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Thereupon, he spoke the six rules for the śikṣamāṇā: "Listen, [Name]!..."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the one who knows and the one who sees—proclaims the six rules of training for the śikṣamāṇā.
"You, Śikṣamāṇā, shall uphold this for as long as you live.

For various reasons, the Buddha rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire; he praised the abandonment of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinction of the fever of desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā enters into the training together with others, yet does not relinquish the precepts, nor manifests the signs of being weak in virtue, and according to her own thoughts she engages in sexual desire even with an animal—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?

He replies, "I am able. "The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, has rebuked the practice of stealing and plundering and praised the practice of not stealing and plundering; one must not transgress even the limit of a single thread, a single inch of cloth, or a single drop of oil."
In this regard, the Buddha has prescribed that the minimum offense is five coins, or the equivalent value of five coins.
If a *śikṣamāṇā* commits an act of theft or robbery, whether she is seized by the king, killed, beaten, bound, banished, or made to pay a fine, or if he says of her:
"You are a thief! You are a child! You are a fool! You have fallen into royal punishment! [she is guilty].
If a śikṣamāṇā steals in this manner, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and destroyed the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can. "The Buddha has, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the taking of life and praised non-killing, stating that one should not kill even an ant, let alone a human being."
If a śikṣamāṇā intentionally takes the life of a human being—whether by handing over a weapon, instructing them to die, or praising death by saying:
"Alas! What is the use of living such a wretched life?"...

"Death is better than life. Following that inclination toward death, he teaches death and praises death through various causes and conditions: whether by means of many killings, or many slaughterings; by setting traps, nets, or snares; by means of *vīdala* (poisoned food) or methods resembling *vīdala*; by suffocating, by causing miscarriage, or by pressing upon the womb; by casting into fire or water, by pushing from a height, or by sending someone on a journey to die; even down to the moment when the two faculties—the body faculty and the life faculty—first arise within the mother’s womb during the *kalala* stage, he employs an evil mind and skillful means to deprive them of their lives.
One who dies due to these causes and conditions is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?

He replied, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and praised the absence of false speech, stating that one should not even speak falsely in jest, much less intentionally.

If a śikṣamāṇā, not knowing and not seeing the empty superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), yet claims: "I know thus, I see thus; I have attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; I have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna; I have attained the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

I have attained the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*); gods have come to me; nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and others have come to me; they question me and I answer them, and I question them and they answer me."
If a śikṣamāṇā speaks such a falsehood, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and destroyed the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?
He replied, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire;
he praised the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinction of the fever of desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind to—whether from the hairline down to the wrists or above the knees—expose her garment and stroke her body upward or downward, embrace, pull, push, lift up, lift down, press, or pinch her; she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
One who has committed such an offense may receive the precepts again.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?
He replied, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire;
he praised the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā, with a mind of leakage, listens to a man with a mind of leakage, grasps his hand or his robe, stands together with him, speaks with him, makes an appointment to enter a secluded place, waits for the man to come, or goes there herself—just as a woman of the white-clad laity does.

These eight matters demonstrate the signs of greedy attachment; such a person is not a śikṣamāṇā, not a śramaṇī, and not a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā, and if she commits them, she must receive the precepts again.
"These matters must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold them?
She replies, "I am able. "Listen, [Name]!
The Saṃgha has already granted you two years of training in the Dharma. A Śikṣamāṇā who upholds the six rules is called a Śikṣamāṇā."
"You have obtained a complete assembly of preceptors and ācāryas, a complete community of bhikṣuṇīs, an excellent land, and an excellent place of practice.
Even the aspirations of a wheel-turning sage king cannot be fully realized, yet you have now attained them all in their entirety.

You should revere the Three Jewels—the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Bhikṣu Saṃgha Jewel; you should make offerings to your preceptor and ācārya, and show respect to those of superior, middling, and inferior standing; and you should diligently apply yourself to the three trainings."
One should train in the precepts, the mind, and wisdom; one should cultivate the three gates of liberation:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should diligently apply oneself to the three activities:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and encouraging the performance of communal affairs.
If you practice this Dharma, you shall open the gate of the Deathless and attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.
Just as a lotus flower grows day and night within the water, so too shall your roots of goodness grow day and night within the Buddha-dharma.
As for the remaining precepts, your preceptor and ācārya shall explain them to you in detail by degrees.
"Within the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, I have already obtained the precepts so difficult to find;
difficult to obtain even in times of no calamity, having now attained them, let them not be in vain.
Prostrating with his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, he circumambulated them to the right and departed with joy.

6. The Text for the Great Bhikṣuṇī Ordination Platform, Part Six. When a śikṣamāṇā first enters among the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, she shall prostrate with her head at the feet of each member of the saṃgha one by one.
Having prostrated at the feet of the monks, the preceptor for the bhikṣuṇīs should instruct her to receive the robes and bowl, and should ask:
"Are these five robes and this bowl yours?
She should reply:
"Yes. He should be instructed to repeat my words: "I, [Name], accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips, which has been cut and sewn.
I, [Name], shall maintain it by not being separated from it overnight."
Thus it is said three times: "I, [Name], accept this *uttarāsaṅga* robe consisting of seven strips, made from two long and one short cut-and-sewn pieces.
I, [Name], shall maintain it by not being separated from it overnight."
Thus it was said three times: "I, [Name], receive this five-piece lower robe (*antarvāsa*), made of one long and one short cut-and-sewn panel.
I, [Name], shall maintain it without being separated from it overnight."
When this has been said three times, if it is a *saṃghāṭī* robe made of patches, one should say:
"I accept and maintain this patched *saṃghāṭī* robe.
The same applies to the other two robes.
“I, [Name], receive this shoulder-covering robe, which is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width.
I, [Name], shall maintain this shoulder-covering robe without being separated from it overnight.”
Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], accept this *kūrpara* robe, four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width.
This *kūrpara*, I, [Name], shall maintain as my constant companion, not parting from it overnight."
Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], shall receive and maintain this pātra of proper measure for constant use.
Thus he says three times.
Next, he instructs him to seek an upādhyāyī: "Venerable One, please take note!"
I, the śikṣamāṇā [Name], request the Venerable One to be my preceptress (upādhyāyinī).
May the Venerable One act as my preceptress, [Name]. Because of this preceptress, may the Saṃgha perform for me, [Name], the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of requesting affiliation with a preceptress.
"Out of compassion.
Thus it is said three times.
The Preceptor should ask: "Are you able to act as the Upādhyāyī for [Name]?"

If a bhikṣuṇī, not knowing and not seeing the empty superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), says of herself: "I know thus, I see thus; I have attained the four fruits and the four paths," up to: "I have attained the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, and fourth dhyāna; I have attained the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I have attained the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*); devas come to me, and nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and so forth come to me; they question me and I answer them, and I question them and they answer me."
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks such a falsehood, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?

[The candidate] replies, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebukes desire, the perception of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire; he praises the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinction of the fever of desire.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind—from the hairline down to the wrists and knees—to pull up her robe and then rub her body either upward or downward, or to embrace, seize, pull, push, lift up, lower down, press, or pinch her, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?

[The candidate] replies, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebukes desire, the perception of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire, while praising the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of desire, listens to a man with a mind of desire as he takes her hand or her robe, stands together with him, converses with him, makes an appointment to enter a secluded and concealed place, waits for the man to come, or goes there herself, she is as one who is like a woman of the lay world.

These eight matters demonstrate the signs of greedy attachment; such a person is not a bhikṣuṇī, not a śramaṇī, and not a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked evil friends and evil associates, while praising virtuous friends and virtuous associates.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, conceals it for even a single night;
and when she knows that the other bhikṣuṇī has either left the order, remained [in her position], been expelled, or departed to a distant place, she says:

"I previously knew this bhikṣuṇī had such a matter, but I did not wish to speak of it to others, nor did I wish to speak of it to the Saṃgha, nor did I wish to let anyone say: [that she had committed such a thing]."
"How can you, sister, defile yourself and [bring shame upon] your elder sister?
She is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?
[The candidate] replies, "I am able. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked evil friends and evil associates while praising virtuous friends and virtuous associates.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the saṃgha of bhikṣus has performed a formal act of unification and has carried out an *adarśana-ukṣepa* (suspension for not recognizing an offense) against a bhikṣu, should follow, assist, and support that bhikṣu—who is alone, without a second, without a companion, and without a partner, neither resting nor ceasing—[she commits an offense].
The bhikṣuṇīs should say this to that bhikṣuṇī:

"The Saṃgha, with one mind and acting in harmony, has performed a formal act of suspension for not seeing [the offense]. This bhikṣu is alone, without a second, without companion, and without partner; he does not cease nor desist. You must not follow him."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the other bhikṣuṇīs admonish her in this manner, persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time so that she may relinquish this matter."
If she relinquishes [the offense] upon the second or third admonition, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"These matters must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; can you maintain them?
He replies, "I can. "Listen, [Name]!
The Sangha has already conferred the full ordination upon you."

You have well received the instruction and followed the teacher’s teaching; you have obtained an excellent upādhyāya and ācārya, an excellent community of monks, and an excellent place for practicing the Path.
Even the aspirations of a Wheel-Turning Sage King cannot be fully realized, yet you have now fulfilled them completely.
You should pay reverent homage to the Three Jewels:
the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Bhikṣu Saṃgha Jewel.
One should diligently practice the three trainings:
the training in virtuous morality, the training in virtuous mind, and the training in virtuous wisdom;
and one should diligently cultivate the three gates of liberation:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should diligently apply oneself to the three activities:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and encouraging the performance of communal affairs.

If you practice this Dharma, you shall open the gate of the Deathless and attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and the path of Pratyekabuddha-hood. Just as a lotus flower grows day and night within the water, so too shall your roots of goodness grow day and night within the Buddha-dharma.
“As for the remaining precepts, the Upādhyāya and Ācārya shall gradually explain them to you in detail.
He then spoke these verses:
“In the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, All that is wondrous and virtuous is gathered.”
Profound and vast, without limit or shore, is this ocean of the jewels of merit.
This was the vow of the Wheel-Turning King and the celestial king Śubhavasu:
"May I always seek to become a śramaṇa; though it was not fulfilled for you, you have now attained it."
Diligently practicing the three types of action, the teachings of the Buddha are of immeasurable kinds;
you should always keep the Dharma in mind and attain all unhindered wisdoms.
Like a lotus flower in the water, it grows and increases day by day.
You too should have such faith, increasing your virtue, learning, concentration, and wisdom.
As for the remaining precepts taught by the Buddha, your preceptor and teachers shall instruct you.
Having completed the circumambulation and prostrations within the assembly, rejoice and each follow your own inclinations.
8. The Text for Receiving the Full Ordination (Upasampadā-karmavācanā). The eighth section on the text for receiving the full ordination. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Regarding the method for receiving the full ordination, one may receive the full ordination when three conditions are present."
"What are the three? First, there is the Saṃgha; second, there is the person who wishes to receive full ordination; third, there is the *karmavācanā*. These are the three.

When the person wishing to receive full ordination first arrives, they should be instructed to perform prostrations at the feet of the Saṃgha in due order. Once they have prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, they should be instructed to receive the robes, and [the preceptor] should ask:
"Is this robe yours? He replied, "It is."

"You should be instructed to repeat my words as follows: 'I, [Name], receive this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] patches, whether it be cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe and not be separated from it overnight.'"
Having said this three times, he then asked: "Is this robe yours? He replied:
"Yes. "I, [Name], receive this *uttarāsaṅga* robe of seven strips, whether it be cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe and not be separated from it overnight."
Having spoken thus three times, he next asks: "Is this robe yours? He replies:
"Yes. "I, [Name], receive this five-piece lower robe (*antaravāsaka*), whether it is cut or uncut; I shall accept and maintain this robe without being separated from it for a night."
Having spoken thus three times, he next asked:
"Is this pātra yours? He replied:
"Yes. "I, [Name], shall accept this *pātra* of standard measure for the purpose of long-term use.
Thus it is said three times.
Having received the robe and bowl, one should seek an upādhyāya and say: "Venerable sir, please take note!
I, [name], request the Venerable sir to be my upādhyāya; may the Venerable sir act as my upādhyāya for the full ordination."
I, [Name], shall receive the full ordination by relying upon the Venerable Preceptor; I pray that the Venerable One will grant me, [Name], the full ordination out of compassion.
Thus he says three times.
The preceptor-teacher should ask: "Who is able to act as the upādhyāya for [Name]?
The upādhyāya replies:
"I, [Name], am able. Immediately, he abandons the state of listening and enters the state of seeing.
The preceptor should then announce to the assembled Saṃgha: "Who is able to act as the instructor for [Name]?"
If there is a bhikṣu among the Saṃgha who says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed as a teacher:

One who teaches out of affection, one who teaches out of anger, one who teaches out of fear, one who teaches out of delusion, and one who does not know what has been taught and what has not been taught—these five qualities being absent, one should be established as a teacher.

One who does not teach out of affection, one who does not teach out of anger, one who does not teach out of fear, one who does not teach out of delusion, and one who knows what has been taught and what has not been taught: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"Venerable Sangha, so-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor so-and-so; so-and-so is able to act as the *karmakāra* (preceptor) for so-and-so.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen: let the Sangha appoint so-and-so as the *karmakāra* to instruct so-and-so."
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor So-and-so; So-and-so is able to act as the *karmakāra* (preceptor) for So-and-so, in order to instruct So-and-so."
"Whichever elders approve that so-and-so shall act as the preceptor to instruct so-and-so, let those elders remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Sangha has already approved that so-and-so shall act as the preceptor to instruct so-and-so."
"Since the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Thereupon, the preceptor goes to the disciple's place and instructs him to bared one shoulder, kneel on his right knee, and join his palms: "Listen, [Name]!..."
Now is the time for ultimate sincerity, the time for truthful speech; later, when questioned likewise within the Saṃgha, you must speak what is true as true and what is untrue as untrue.
I now ask you: Are you a man? Have you reached the age of twenty?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not working as a laborer for others?
Were you not purchased?
"Are you not one who has broken the precepts?
Are you not a government official?
Have you not been involved in government affairs?"
Have you not plotted against the royal family?
Have you not incurred debts to others?
As for a man's diseases, do you have any such as leprosy, abscesses, discharges, scrofula, consumption, or epilepsy?
"Do you have parents living?
If you say they do, have your parents given you permission to go forth?
Have you not previously been a bhikṣu?"
If you say that you have performed [the ordination], have you maintained the precepts with purity?
When relinquishing the precepts, did you restore them according to the Dharma with a single-minded focus?
Are the three robes and the alms bowl complete?
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor? He replied:
"I am named [Name], and my preceptor is named [Name].
Having finished questioning the teacher, one should announce to the Saṃgha:
"I have finished questioning [Name]."
The preceptor says:
"If you are pure, bring her forward.
He instructs her to prostrate at the feet of the Sangha; having prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, she requests the full ordination from the Sangha, saying: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
I, [Name], seek to receive the full ordination from the preceptor [Name].
I, [Name], now request the Saṃgha to grant me the full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor.
"May the Saṃgha deliver me; please grant the full ordination to me, [Name].
Out of compassion.
Thus he says three times.
Immediately, a bhikṣu shall announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor, seeks to receive full ordination.
So-and-so has already requested the Saṃgha for full ordination, with So-and-so as preceptor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall now inquire among the Saṃgha regarding [the candidate] so-and-so concerning the obstructing dharmas.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The text for the Preceptor’s inquiry regarding the obstructing dharmas is identical to the text for the Teacher’s inquiry regarding the obstructing dharmas mentioned above.
The former [case] was by means of emptiness and stillness; this is different only in that it is done amidst the assembly. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Is there anyone who has not yet asked?
If there is anyone who has not yet asked, they should ask now; those who have already asked should remain silent."
The Preceptor shall proclaim: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so, with So-and-so as his preceptor, seeks to receive the full ordination.
So-and-so has already requested the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with So-and-so as his preceptor."
So-and-so declares himself pure and free from obstacles; his age is complete, his robes and bowl are in full possession, and So-and-so is his preceptor.
If the time has come for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, may the Sangha confer the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as his preceptor.
Thus he makes the formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor, seeks to receive full ordination."
So-and-so has already requested the full ordination from the Sangha, with So-and-so as preceptor.
So-and-so has personally declared that he is pure and free from all obstacles, that his age is complete, and that his robes and bowl are complete; So-and-so is the preceptor, So-and-so.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
Which Elders consent to confer the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor? Those who consent, let them remain silent;
those who do not consent, let them speak.
"Has this first *karmavācanā* been accomplished?
Thus it is said three times: "The Saṃgha has already granted its consent; the full ordination for [Name] has been completed, with [Name] as preceptor."
"Since the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If someone asks: "How old are you?"
It should be said that there is no such thing as a "year. When?
Whether it be winter, spring, or summer—whether with an intercalary month or without one—at these seasonal intervals, you should maintain mindfulness for as long as you live.
Immediately, one should recite the four reliances: “Listen, [Name]!

This Buddha Bhagavān Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the four reliances for those receiving full ordination; by relying upon these, one may leave the household life, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu.”
What are the four?
"Relying on rag-robes.
By relying on this, a bhikṣu attains renunciation and receives full ordination, thereby fulfilling the dharma of a bhikṣu."

If one further obtains white flaxen cloth, red flaxen cloth, kāya cloth, kauseya cloth, śāṇa cloth, kṣaumaka cloth, or cotton cloth—such other pure garments as these—all are permitted to be kept as surplus.
"In this regard, can you maintain the practice of wearing rag-robes for as long as you live?
"I can. "In reliance on alms-gathering, a bhikṣu is able to go forth, receive full ordination, and fulfill the dharma of a bhikṣu."

If one further obtains food prepared for them, such as food provided on the six fast days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), food on the first day of the month, food on the sixteenth day, communal monastic food (*saṃghika-bhakta*), food from a private room, or food offered by invitation—whether to the community as a whole or to individuals—these and other such pure foods are all considered "excess" (*atireka*) and may be accepted.
"In this regard, can one rely on alms-gathering for as long as life lasts?
He replied, "Yes. "One relies on dwelling at the foot of a tree.
By relying on these, a bhikṣu attains the going forth and receives full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu."

If one obtains a heated room, a lecture hall, a palace, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, a gabled house, a flat-roofed house, an earthen cave, a mountain cave, or bedding such as *pāduka*, *maṇḍalaka*, or *caṇḍalaka*—down to even grass mats or leaf mats—and other such pure dwellings and bedding, all of these may be accepted as surplus.
"Among these, can one dwell relying on staying under a tree and make use of it for as long as life lasts?
"Yes, one can. "Relying on discarded medicine, a bhikṣu may go forth and receive full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu."
Furthermore, if one obtains the four kinds of medicinal substances for melting and clarifying— clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar— and the four kinds of pure fats—
bear fat, donkey fat, pig fat, and sturgeon fat— as well as the five kinds of root medicines—
śalī, ginger, red aconite, pāṭhā, and kando root— and the five kinds of fruit medicines— *a-* [the text here is truncated].
Emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), belleric myrobalan (*vibhītaka*), yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*), black pepper (*marica*), and *babbāla*;
five kinds of salt: black salt, white salt, purple salt, red salt, and rock salt;
five kinds of decoctions: decoctions of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and five kinds of resin.
Yakṣīraka, sājara, tyej, tyejabhadi, tyejabhana—
these and other such pure medicinal herbs are all obtained in abundance.
"In this regard, may you rely on discarded medicine for use throughout your life?
He replies, "I can. "Listen, [Name]!
This Buddha, the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the four *pārājika* dharmas for fully ordained bhikṣus."

If a bhikṣu commits any one of these four *pārājika* offenses, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Just as when a tāla tree is cut down, it does not grow again, nor does it become green, tall, or broad;

so too is it with a bhikṣu: if he commits any one of the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣu.

"The Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked sensual desire, sensual perceptions, sensual thoughts, and the fever of sensual desire; he praised the severing of desire, the removal of sensual perceptions, and the extinguishing of the fever of sensual desire."

If a bhikṣu, having entered into the disciplinary rules together with other bhikṣus, does not relinquish the precepts, nor manifests the signs of being "weak in virtue," yet according to his own thoughts engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—then he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
"This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it? He replied, "I am able.

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the act of stealing and plundering the Dharma and praised the practice of not stealing or plundering. This applies even to a single thread, a single inch of cloth, or a single drop of oil; one must not steal or plunder these, nor anything else down to the smallest measure. Within this, the Buddha established a minimum limit of five coins, or whatever is equivalent in value to five coins.
If a bhikṣu, regarding the matter of what he has stolen or plundered, is seized by the king, or executed, or beaten, or bound, or banished, or fined, and says:
"You are a thief! You are a child! You are a fool! You have fallen into official punishment!"
"If a bhikṣu steals or seizes in this manner, he is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, not a son of the Śākya; he has fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣu.
This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; can you uphold it?"
He replied, "The Buddha has, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the taking of life and praised non-killing; one should not kill even an ant, let alone a human being."
If a bhikṣu takes the life of a person with his own hand, or provides a knife, or instructs them to die or praises death, saying:
"Ho! Man, what is the use of living this evil life?"
"Death is superior to life.

Following that inclination toward death, he teaches death and praises death through various causes and conditions: whether by means of *ūta* (poisoning), *śīrṣa* (blows to the head), setting snares, setting nets, or using traps; whether by means of *vīdala* (mechanical killing), *vīdalopama* (killing like a mechanical device), cutting off the breath, causing an abortion, pressing on the abdomen, throwing into fire or water, pushing down from a height, or sending someone on a journey to die; even down to the moment the two faculties—the body faculty and the life faculty—first arise within the mother’s womb during the *kalala* stage, he employs an evil mind and skillful means to deprive them of their lives.
One who dies because of such causes and conditions is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya; they have lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣu.
This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; are you able to uphold it?

He replied, "The Buddha has, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and praised truthful speech. Within this context, one should not even speak falsely in jest, let alone intentionally tell lies."

If a bhikṣu neither knows nor sees the supramundane states that are empty, yet claims, "I know thus and see thus; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat; I have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; I have attained the immeasurable states of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I have attained the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing."
The devas come to me; the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and so forth come to me. They question me and I answer them; I question them and they answer me.
If a bhikṣu speaks such false speech, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣu.
This matter must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts; can you uphold it?
He replied, "Listen, [Name]! An offense of the first category cannot be rectified;
as for an offense of the second category, although it can be rectified, for however long it was concealed, you must undergo *parivāsa* for that duration."

Having completed the *parivāsa*, one should undergo the *mānatva* for six nights; having completed the *mānatva*, one is rehabilitated (*abbhāna*) before an assembly of twenty bhikṣus. Within that assembly, this constitutes a cause for shame and being held in contempt by others.
"In this regard, you must not intentionally stimulate the organ to emit semen; can you refrain from doing such a thing?
[He] replied, "I can. "You must not intentionally touch the body of a woman."
One must not speak harsh words to women.
One must not praise one's own body before women for the sake of offerings.
One must not act as a matchmaker for women.
One must not build a private dwelling for oneself; the Buddha has prescribed what may be built and what may not be built.
One must not build a large dwelling; the Buddha has prescribed what may be built and what may not be built.
One must not slander others on account of a rootless offense;
one must not slander another by claiming a minor offense is grave due to its causes and conditions;
and one must not strive to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
One must not assist those who cause schisms in the Sangha;
one must not bring disgrace upon other families;
and one must not be perverse in nature or difficult to instruct.
"Can such a matter not be done?
He replied, "It can. "Listen, [Name]!
The Sangha has already conferred the full ordination upon you."

You have well received the instruction and followed the teacher’s teaching; you have obtained a good preceptor and ācārya, a good community of monks, and a fine land and place for practicing the Path.
Even the aspirations of a Wheel-Turning Sage King cannot be fully realized, yet you have now fulfilled them completely.
You should revere the Three Jewels:
the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Saṅgha Jewel of Bhikṣus.
One should diligently practice the three trainings:
the training in virtuous ethics, the training in virtuous mind, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
One should diligently cultivate the three gates of liberation:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
You should diligently apply yourself to the three activities:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and encouraging others to perform communal tasks.

If you practice this Dharma, you shall open the gate of the Deathless and attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, and the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Just as a lotus flower grows day and night within the water, so too shall your roots of goodness grow day and night within the Buddha-dharma.
As for the remaining precepts, your preceptor and ācārya shall explain them to you in detail by degrees.
He then spoke these verses for him:
“Within the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, All that is wondrous and good is gathered;
Profound, vast, and boundless, It is an ocean of jewels of merit.”
This vow was made by the Wheel-Turning Kings and the Celestial Kings, the Kings of the Good Dharma;
they constantly sought to become śramaṇas, yet did not achieve it, whereas you have already attained it.
Through diligent practice of the three karmas, the teachings of the Buddha are of immeasurable kinds.
You should constantly recollect the Dharma, And attain all unhindered wisdoms.
Like a lotus flower in the water, Gradually increasing day by day,
So too shall you, through faith, Increase in virtue, learning, concentration, and wisdom.
"The remaining precepts taught by the Buddha Should be instructed by the Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
Having completed the prostrations and circumambulations within the assembly, May you rejoice and each follow your own inclinations.
9. Text for Binding a Small Boundary (Kṣudrasīmābandhana-vākya) First, bind the boundary of the open space, and thereafter bind the boundary of the precinct.

First, a bhikṣu proclaims the boundaries of the small boundary for the four directions to establish the limits; then, he performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) in the midst of the assembly, making this announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"Venerable sirs, the monk so-and-so proclaims the boundaries of the small precinct in the four directions. The Saṃgha now establishes a small precinct to create a *karmavācanā* site (*sīmāmaṇḍala*).

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall establish a small precinct within these four directional boundaries to create a *karmavācanā* site."
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu so-and-so has proclaimed the marks of the small boundary (sīmā) on the four sides. The Saṃgha now intends to establish a small boundary within these four-sided marks to create a *karmavastu* (ordination site)."
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a small boundary (sīmā) within these four marks to create a *śīlā-maṇḍala* (precept platform), let them remain silent;
those who do not consent, let them speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to establish a small boundary within these four marks to form a *karmavācanā* site (*sīmāmaṇḍala*).
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such."

10. The Text for Binding the Great Boundary (Mahā-sīmā-bandhana-vastu). This tenth section on binding the great boundary first requires one bhikṣu to proclaim the characteristics of the four sides of the great boundary and establish the limits. Once this has been done, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) is performed in the midst of the assembly. The motion is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣu [Name] proclaims the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) on all four sides; that which is within these marks is within the boundary.
If the Saṃgha deems the time has come, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, establish a single boundary for the common residence and the Uposatha within this area.
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Bhikṣu [Name] has proclaimed the marks of the great boundary of the four directions; that which is within these marks is the interior of the boundary. Within this, a single boundary for the common residence and the *poṣadha* is being established."
"Whichever elders approve of this single *poṣadha* communal residence boundary, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved the single *poṣadha* communal residence boundary."
"Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld. 11.

Regarding the communal residence for a single poṣadha: within whatever extent of boundary has been established, one excludes the village and its surrounding territory, taking instead the open space and the dwelling site.

“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Within the limits of a single boundary established for a common residence for a single *poṣadha*, excluding villages and village boundaries, taking only the open space and the dwelling sites—within this boundary for a common residence for a single *poṣadha*, we shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of ‘not being separated from one’s robes while staying overnight.’”

"Whichever elders among you consent to this formal act (*kamma*) for not being separated from one's robes while staying overnight within the boundary established for a single *poṣadha* communal residence, let those elders remain silent;
whoever does not consent, let them speak."
"The Saṃgha has already consented to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for staying overnight without one's robe within the boundary of a common residence for a single *poṣadha*.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

12. The Text for Resolving the Great Boundary (Mahā-sīmā). The text for resolving the small boundary (Kṣudra-sīmā) also relies on this same text; the only difference is that one should explicitly state "small boundary. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
In this matter, regarding the common residence for a single *poṣadha* and the harmonious assembly, one shall dissolve the boundary and relinquish the boundary.

If the Saṃgha deems it the right time, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant permission to dissolve the boundary and relinquish the boundary for the common residence of a single *poṣadha*.
Thus he makes the motion: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Within this single boundary for the common residence for the Poṣadha, we shall dissolve the boundary and relinquish the boundary."

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the dissolution of the boundary and the relinquishing of the boundary for a single *poṣadha* at this common residence remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Sangha has consented to the dissolution of the boundary and the relinquishing of the boundary for a single *poṣadha* at this common residence."
“Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The reason there is no separate text for the boundary of the robes is that if one wishes to further enlarge or contract the boundary, one should first dissolve the boundary of the robes and then dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*);

if one dissolves the great boundary directly, the boundary of the robes will also be removed along with it, and thus there is no need for a cumbersome text. The texts for the nuns’ establishment and relinquishment of boundaries are the same.
